records.title: Active Exhaust Valve Seizure and Cable Rot (VR-4)
records.description: Early VR-4s have an Active Exhaust System with a driver-selectable Tour/Sport valve in the rear exhaust; the system was phased out after the 1994 model year. The valve shaft corrodes and seizes (usually stuck in the quiet Tour position) and the actuator cable rots away, so toggling the switch changes nothing. The valve's D-shaped shaft rounds off so the external lever can move while the internal plate stays shut, and the sealed assembly cannot be easily disassembled for repair.
records.solution: Free a seized valve with extended penetrating-oil soaks and careful heat cycles — a well-documented community procedure — and replace the rotted actuator cable, or fit a replacement/used valve assembly. Many owners simply wire the valve open or delete it with an aftermarket exhaust.
symptoms: No exhaust tone change when switching between Tour and Sport
Exhaust permanently quiet and restrictive (valve stuck in Tour)
Active exhaust switch light works but nothing happens
Corroded or detached actuator cable at the rear muffler valve

records.title: AWD Transfer Case Oil Leak Leading to Bearing Failure and Driveline Lockup (VR-4)
records.description: The all-wheel-drive transfer case on early 3000GT VR-4 models can leak gear oil past its seals and O-rings, and because the unit holds very little fluid, even a slow leak starves the bearings. NHTSA issued two recalls for this defect (93V-033 and 02V-143) because bearing failure can lock the entire drivetrain without warning at highway speed, causing loss of vehicle control. Many cars never received the recall reseal, and 3si.org forum threads document failures decades later.
records.solution: Check whether recalls 93V033000 and 02V143 were performed (the 2002 remedy installed a reseal kit and replaced damaged cases). Otherwise, have the transfer case resealed at the first sign of leakage and inspect/top off the fluid regularly; a case showing bearing or gear damage must be replaced.
symptoms: Gear oil spots under the middle of the car
Burnt gear-oil smell after driving
Whining or growling from beneath the floor that rises with speed
Driveline binding or shudder in tight turns
Sudden grinding or lockup from the drivetrain

records.title: ECU Electrolytic Capacitor Leakage Causing Stalling and No-Start (1991-1993)
records.description: The electrolytic capacitors inside 1991-1993 ECUs leak corrosive electrolyte with age and heat cycling, eating copper traces off the circuit board. The result is erratic running, stalling, intermittent or complete no-start, and — if left long enough — an unrepairable ECU. The 3000GT/Stealth community considers preventive recapping mandatory on any unrepaired first-generation car; a telltale fishy 'rotten seafood' odor from the center console means electrolyte is already escaping.
records.solution: Remove the ECU and have the three electrolytic capacitors replaced (about $1 each in parts, or $100-300 at an electronics/ECU repair service), with board trace repair if electrolyte damage has started. Recap proactively before symptoms appear — a board with eaten traces may need a replacement ECU.
symptoms: Intermittent hard start or no-start
Engine stalling or sudden power loss while driving
Erratic idle and random driveability glitches

Rapid clicking or chattering from under the dash

records.title: Front Brake Hose Cracking at Full Steering Lock (NHTSA Recall 96V-143)
records.description: On 1991-1994 cars, the front wheel-side brake hoses can crack when the steering is at full lock with the suspension at full travel, leaking brake fluid. records.solution: Mitsubishi's recall remedy replaced both front wheel-side hoses with revised assemblies; verify recall completion by VIN. On any car still wearing original rubber hoses, replace all four brake hoses with new OEM or stainless-braided lines.

records.title: Getrag AWD Manual Transmission Synchro Wear and Gear Grind (VR-4 5-Speed/6-Speed)
records.description: The Getrag-built AWD gearboxes in the VR-4 (W5MG1 5-speed through 1993, W6MG1 6-speed from 1994) are notorious for worn synchronizers, especially 1st-2nd and 2nd-3rd, causing grinding shifts. The synchros are undersized for the mass of the gears at high engine speed, so spirited driving wears them quickly; continuing to drive through the grind chews up gears and sliders, many of which are no longer available new. Rebuilds require specialist knowledge and parts kits from community vendors.
records.solution: Rebuild the transmission with updated synchro kits (R'venge Performance, Jack's Transmissions and similar specialists supply parts) at the first sign of regular grinding, before gear and slider damage compounds the bill. Use the correct fluid and double-clutch or slow shifts to extend synchro life in the meantime.

records.title: Hydraulic Lash Adjuster 'Lifter Tick' on the 6G72 V6
records.description: The 6G72's hydraulic lash adjusters are prone to internal varnish buildup and wear, producing the platform's famous ticking noise at idle that rises with RPM. Dirty oil or extended change intervals make the adjusters bleed down and stick, increasing valvetrain clearance. It is mostly an annoyance, but a chronically loud, sticking adjuster accelerates rocker and cam lobe wear over time.
records.solution: Start with frequent oil changes and a cleaning additive regimen (community-proven options include a Rislone or Lucas treatment cycle, or pulling and cleaning the adjusters); persistent tick is cured by replacing the 24 lash adjusters, with upgraded 'big bore' Gen3 lifters or solid-lifter conversions sold specifically for this engine.
symptoms: Rhythmic ticking from the top of the engine at idle
Tick frequency increases with engine RPM
Noise is loudest at cold start and may fade when warm

records.title: Pop-Up Headlight Motor and ETACS Failures (1991-1993)
records.description: Pre-facelift cars use motorized pop-up headlights controlled by the ETACS body module, and after 30+ years the motors, internal position switches, fuses, and ETACS relays commonly fail. Lights stick up, stick down, raise slowly, or only one side operates (the classic 'wink'). Because the motor always spins one direction and is stopped by a position switch inside the assembly, diagnosis confuses many owners — replacing a motor alone often does not fix it.
records.solution: Diagnose systematically: try the manual pop-up button (if it works there but not from the headlight switch, suspect the column switch; if neither works, test the fuse, motor, internal position switch, and ETACS unit). Used motors and ETACS repairs are the usual fix; a manual knob under the hood raises the lights as a roadside workaround.
symptoms: One or both headlights will not raise or retract
One headlight stuck up while the other works (the 'wink')
Slow, jerky, or grinding headlight movement

records.title: Timing Belt and Hydraulic Tensioner Failure Destroying the Interference DOHC 6G72
records.description: The DOHC 24-valve 6G72 in the SL and VR-4 is an interference engine: if the timing belt snaps or the known-weak hydraulic tensioner bleeds down and lets the belt skip teeth, pistons strike open valves. Documented failures have bent as many as 17 of the engine's 24 valves, turning a missed $1,000 service into a $3,000-5,000 cylinder head job. Oil from leaking cam seals or valve covers contaminating the belt accelerates failure, and the cramped transverse V6 layout makes the 60,000-mile/5-year service frequently deferred.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt, hydraulic tensioner, idler pulleys, and water pump as a set every 60,000 miles or 5 years, fixing any cam/crank seal oil leaks at the same time. On a car with unknown service history, do the belt service before driving the car hard.
symptoms: Ticking, whirring, or slapping noise from the front timing cover
Engine cranks freely but will not start after a belt failure
Sudden rough running or misfires after the belt skips teeth
Oil seepage around the timing covers contaminating the belt
Unknown or overdue belt service history

records.title: VR-4 4WS Rear Steering Pump and Hard Line Leaks
records.description: The all-wheel-steering (4WS) system on the 1991-1996 VR-4 (and select 1991-1993 SL trims) uses a dedicated rear-mounted hydraulic pump driven off the rear-differential pinion. The pump's flanged metal feed line is mounted under the car and rusts heavily over time. When the line corrodes through or the pump seal fails, owners lose all 4WS fluid quickly, trigger the 4WS warning light, and can even lose front power steering assist because the system shares a fluid reservoir. Replacement is brutal because the bolted-on hard line is not sold separately - a full new rear pump assembly runs ~$900+ and parts can take 3 months to source.
records.solution: Inspect the flanged feed/return line at the rear pump for rust and weeping. For small low-pressure leaks, cut out the corroded section and bridge with high-pressure hose and double-clamped fittings as a temporary fix. For high-pressure-side or pump-internal leaks, the proper repair requires dropping the rear subframe to access the pump (parts ~$900 OEM, labor 6-10 hours). Many long-term VR-4 owners install a 4WS delete kit with block-off plates that bypasses the rear pump and hard-locks the rear steering rack, eliminating the failure point entirely ($150-$400 in parts).
symptoms: 4WS warning light illuminated on dashboard
Puddle of red/amber power steering fluid under rear of vehicle
Power steering reservoir empties repeatedly
Loss of front power steering assist (shared reservoir)
Whining noise from rear pump area
Visible rust or wet residue on the hard line at the back of the rear pump

records.title: 1G ECU Electrolytic Capacitor Leakage (Rough Idle, No-Start)
records.description: The electrolytic capacitors in 1990-1994 ECUs have defective seals and leak electrolyte onto the circuit board, corroding traces and surface-mount components — 1990-1993 units are worst, and the front capacitor in 1990 ECUs is known to short and burn through the board under it, taking out the idle speed control circuit. The leaked electrolyte keeps eating the board over time, so an untouched 30-year-old ECU is assumed to need this repair.
records.solution: Have the ECU recapped: replace all electrolytic capacitors, neutralize and clean the electrolyte residue, and repair any damaged traces (especially the ISC traces). Specialist shops such as ECMTuning offer this service; capable DIYers can do it with basic soldering equipment.

Random stalling

records.title: 2G Fuel Pump Wiring Voltage Drop and Fuel Pump/MFI Relay Failure
records.description: On 1995-1999 cars the fuel pump's factory wiring is undersized and its chassis ground (at the floor crossmember under the driver's seat) corrodes with age, dropping voltage at the pump into the 10-11V range under load. The paired fuel pump/MFI relay behind the center console can also fail. The result is intermittent cranking no-starts (no pump prime), stalling, and lean stumble or fuel cut at wide-open throttle on turbo cars — a problem so common the community-standard fix is the documented 'fuel pump rewire.'
records.solution: Test voltage at the pump and the fuel pump/MFI relay first; replace the relay if it fails continuity testing, and repair or supplement the corroded ground wire. The accepted long-term fix is the DSM fuel pump rewire: a relay-triggered, fused 12-gauge feed direct from the battery/alternator with a fresh chassis ground.
symptoms: Engine cranks but fuel pump never hums
Intermittent no-start, often after heat soak
Stalling or dying while driving
Lean stumble or fuel cut at wide-open throttle
Fuel pressure/voltage at the pump drops under load

records.title: 4G63 7-Bolt Crank Walk (Thrust Bearing Failure)
records.description: The 1995-1999 Eclipse GS-T and GSX use the 7-bolt 4G63 turbo engine, which is notoriously prone to 'crank walk' — excessive axial movement of the crankshaft caused by thrust bearing failure. The crankshaft literally moves fore-and-aft inside the block, eventually destroying the crank position sensor backplate and ruining the crank, block, and bearings. Root causes include factory-misadjusted clutch hydraulics leaving residual pressure on the thrust bearing, 7-bolt oil squirter design that bleeds pressure from main bearing feeds, and a metallurgically weaker crank than the earlier 6-bolt motor. Crankwalk was most prevalent in engines built in 1995, and most affected units failed at low mileage before the first timing belt service. There is no recall, and full repair requires a complete engine teardown with crank and bearing replacement.
records.solution: Confirm with a dial indicator on the crank snout while a helper presses the clutch (>0.010" axial movement = crank walk). The only durable fix is to pull the engine, replace the crankshaft, all main/rod/thrust bearings, and ideally install ARP main studs with dowels. Mitigation while diagnosing: verify clutch master/slave cylinder adjustment so there is zero residual pressure on the throwout bearing at rest, and disable the clutch interlock switch so drivers do not rest a foot on the clutch. Plugging the 7-bolt piston oil squirters is a common preventive modification during a rebuild.
symptoms: Ticking or clicking noise from timing belt / crank pulley area
Clutch engagement/disengagement point changes (especially on left turns)
Clutch pedal sticks down or feels inconsistent
Engine stalls or briefly cuts out when clutch is held in
Repeated crank position sensor (CKP) failures
Visible fore/aft movement of crankshaft pulley when clutch is operated

records.title: 4G63 "Crankwalk" - Crankshaft Thrust Bearing Failure (7-bolt engines)
records.description: The 1996-1999 second-generation Eclipse turbo (GS-T/GSX) uses the 7-bolt 4G63T, which is notorious for "crankwalk": the crankshaft thrust bearing wears out and allows the crank to move excessively fore-aft (lateral end-play). Marginal oiling to the thrust surface, dirt contamination, and heavy-duty clutch pressure loads accelerate the wear. As the crank walks it destroys the crankshaft position/timing signal and eventually the crankshaft itself. It is one of the most feared failures in the DSM community and is largely non-repairable without pulling the engine. The earlier 1990-1994 1G and 1995 6-bolt engines are far less prone; Mitsubishi revised the thrust bearing design (culminating in a 4-piece self-aligning thrust bearing by 1999) to mitigate it, but 1996-early-1997 cars remain high-risk.
records.solution: There is no reliable in-car fix. Diagnosis is by measuring crankshaft end-play with a dial indicator (spec is roughly 0.002-0.010 in; more than that indicates walk). Once diagnosed, the remedy is an engine rebuild or replacement with a machined/align-honed block and new thrust bearings, ideally converting to a stronger 6-bolt crank/block or using an updated split thrust bearing. Owners reduce risk with frequent oil changes, avoiding overly aggressive clutches, and not launching the car hard.
symptoms: Ticking or knocking from the timing/pulley side of the engine
Erratic idle or stalling as the crank/cam timing signal is disrupted
No-start or intermittent start
Visible fore-aft movement of the crank pulley
Fluctuating ignition timing on a light

records.title: AWD (GSX) Transfer Case Lockup - NHTSA Recall 98V069000
records.description: The all-wheel-drive Eclipse GSX was recalled (NHTSA campaign 98V069, March 1998) covering 1990-1998 GSX models. A brass plug in the center of the transfer case yoke can leak, causing insufficient lubrication in the transfer case; the transfer case can then lock up, which can cause loss of vehicle control and a crash. Roughly 24,275 vehicles were covered. Beyond the recall itself, the AWD driveline (transfer case, center differential, rear diff, and pressed-in rear wheel bearings) is a known wear area on these cars, especially if fluids were neglected.
records.solution: Under the original recall, dealers inspected transfer case oil volume, checked for leakage at the yoke plug, and inspected for operational degradation, repairing as needed at no charge. On a used car today, verify the recall was performed, keep the transfer case and differential fluids fresh (gear oil per spec), and address any yoke/output-seal leaks promptly. A failed transfer case requires rebuild or replacement; worn rear AWD wheel bearings are pressed and typically replaced as a bearing or complete hub.

Whining or howling from the driveline
Gear oil leak at the transfer case yoke/output
Vibration or driveline shudder
Rear wheel bearing growl/rumble that changes with speed

records.title: Balance Shaft Belt Failure Destroying the Timing Belt (Interference 4G63)
records.description: The turbo 4G63 is an interference engine, and its narrow balance shaft belt runs directly alongside the main timing belt. When the aging balance shaft belt frays or snaps — common on neglected 1G six-bolt and 2G seven-bolt cars — the debris gets caught in the timing belt, causing it to jump teeth or break outright. Because the pistons and valves share the same space, the result is at least eight bent valves and a cylinder head rebuild, and the DSM community treats overdue belts as the single most engine-destroying maintenance lapse on these cars.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt, balance shaft belt, tensioners, and idlers together every 60,000 miles, never leaving an old balance shaft belt in place behind a new timing belt. Many owners permanently remove the balance shafts with a balance shaft elimination kit (stub shaft) so the failure-prone belt is deleted entirely.

Engine cranks freely but will not restart
Flapping or slapping noise from the front timing cover
Visible fraying or missing teeth on belts behind the timing cover
Low oil pressure if the oil pump/balance shaft drive is disturbed

records.title: Cam Angle Sensor (CAS) / Optical Distributor Failure - No-Start and Stalling
records.description: The 4G63 uses a cam angle sensor (an optical sensor mounted in the distributor housing on the exhaust cam) to provide the crank/cam timing signal to the ECU. With age the CAS optical disc, LEDs/phototransistors, and internal bearing wear out and produce erratic or lost signals. On 1G cars the CAS is base-timing adjustable; on 2G it is fixed. Failure is a classic cause of intermittent no-start, hot-soak no-start, and random stalling on these cars, and it can be intermittent enough that tapping the sensor temporarily restores it. It is frequently misdiagnosed. (Note: crankwalk can mimic these symptoms by physically disturbing the CAS drive.)
records.solution: Diagnose by checking for spark and injector pulse and verifying the CAS output signal on a scope/meter; a bearing that has play or a signal that cuts out when hot confirms it. Replace the cam angle sensor (or the complete optical distributor assembly). On 1G cars, re-set base ignition timing after replacement. Ensure grounds and the connector are clean, as poor grounds mimic CAS faults.
symptoms: Intermittent no-start / crank but no spark
Hot-start failure (won't restart until it cools)
Random stalling while driving
Rough running that comes and goes

records.title: Front Lower Ball Joint Boot Damage and Separation (NHTSA Recalls 99V066001 / 00V421001)
records.description: Mitsubishi issued two recalls (99V066001, then the expanded 00V421001) on 2G Eclipses because the rubber boots on the front lower lateral arm ball joints were damaged during assembly, letting dirt and water into the joint. records.title: Front Subframe / Crossmember and Rocker Rust Corrosion (salt-belt cars)
records.description: Like most DSM-era cars, 1990s Eclipses in road-salt regions suffer structural corrosion of the front crossmember/subframe (which locates the lower control arms) as well as the rocker panels, strut towers, and rear subframe/trailing-arm mounts. Because the lower control arms bolt to the front crossmember, severe perforation can allow a control arm to loosen or detach, causing loss of control - the same failure mode Mitsubishi later addressed with formal crossmember-corrosion recalls on newer models (the cited bulletin/recall covers other Mitsubishi models and is referenced here as an analogous failure mode). On these 25-35 year-old cars it is a safety and roadworthiness concern rather than a warranty item, and heavily rusted examples are common in the Northeast/Midwest.
records.solution: Inspect the crossmember, control-arm mounts, subframe, and rockers for perforation, using a punch/hammer test on suspect areas (perforation means replacement). Repair options are welding in new steel/reinforcement plates by a competent shop or replacing the crossmember/subframe with a sound used or reproduction unit. Undercoating and keeping drains clear slows further corrosion. Do not drive a car with a perforated control-arm mount.

Clunking or loose feel from the front suspension

records.title: Lifter Tick from Hydraulic Lash Adjusters
records.description: The 4G63's hydraulic lash adjusters (lifters) are notorious for clogging with oil varnish or bleeding down, producing the infamous DSM 'lifter tick' from the valve cover. The early-design lifters used in 1G cars were revised twice by Mitsubishi specifically to address the noise. Forum consensus is that the tick itself rarely damages the engine — many owners drive with it for years — but it is loud, persistent, and frequently mistaken for rod knock or other serious problems.
records.solution: Start with a fresh oil change at the correct viscosity; if the tick persists, remove and clean the lash adjusters or replace them with the revised Mitsubishi parts (MD337687/MD377054) or current aftermarket equivalents. New lifters must be bled before installation, and may need 20-30 minutes of running to quiet down fully.

Noise loudest at cold start
Tick speeds up with engine RPM
Noise changes with oil brand, weight, or oil age
Tick persists after engine is fully warm

records.title: V6 Engine Oil Consumption
records.description: The 3.0L 6G72 and 3.8L 6G75 V6 engines in the Eclipse GT develop excessive oil consumption over time. Worn valve stem seals and piston ring glazing allow oil to enter the combustion chambers, producing blue exhaust smoke and requiring frequent top-offs.
records.solution: Replace valve stem seals as a first step. If consumption persists, the piston rings may need replacement. Use high-mileage synthetic oil with seal conditioners. Monitor oil level every 1,000 miles.

records.title: Rust at Rear Wheel Arches, Lower Quarter Panels, and Rockers
records.description: Both 1G and 2G Eclipse/Talon bodies rot in predictable places: the rear wheel arches and the lower quarter panel just ahead of the rear tires, the rocker/support area under the doors, and — most structurally serious — the front strut towers. The arch and rocker seams trap road salt and moisture between panel layers, so by the time paint bubbles appear the rust has usually perforated multiple layers from the inside out. Forum consensus treats the rear lower wheel wells and strut towers as the first places to inspect on any survivor car.
records.solution: Cut out perforated metal and weld in patch panels or replacement quarter/arch sections, then seam-seal and rustproof the cavities; surface treatment alone does not stop inside-out rot. Eclipse and Talon steel body panels of the same generation interchange, which widens the supply of donor sheet metal. Strut tower rust requires professional structural repair.
symptoms: Bubbling paint on the rear wheel arch lips
Holes in the lower quarter panels ahead of the rear tires
Crusty or perforated rocker panels under the doors
Rust flakes or perforation around the front strut towers
Rust where the rear quarter meets the bumper cover

records.title: Timing Belt Failure on Interference 4G63 (catastrophic valve damage)
records.description: The DOHC 4G63 (both the naturally aspirated 4G63 and turbo 4G63T across 1990-1999) is an interference engine: if the timing belt snaps or jumps, the pistons strike the open valves, bending valves and often damaging the head and pistons. These belts were specified for replacement around 60,000 miles, and on 30-year-old cars many have been neglected or the balance-shaft belt has been ignored. The 4G63 also drives the oil pump off a balance shaft, so a failed balance-shaft belt can wrap around and knock the timing belt off, causing the same catastrophic result. This is the single most important preventive-maintenance item on any 1990s Eclipse.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt, tensioner, idler pulley, and water pump as a set every 60k miles (or on any car of unknown history). Replace the balance-shaft belt at the same time or perform a balance-shaft delete done correctly (retaining oil-pump drive) per accepted DSM practice. If a belt has already failed, repair requires removing the head for a valve job (new/straightened valves, guides, seals, machining) and inspecting the pistons - frequently 4-8 bent intake valves are found.
symptoms: Sudden loss of power / engine dies while driving and will not restart
Engine cranks but does not fire
No compression on cranking
Rattling or slapping noise before failure from a worn belt/tensioner
Resistance when turning the crank by hand (valves contacting pistons)

records.title: Timing Belt Tensioner and Water Pump Failure
records.description: The Eclipse timing belt tensioner hydraulic damper fails, allowing the timing belt to become loose and potentially jump teeth. The water pump, driven by the timing belt, also develops bearing failure and coolant leaks. These failures are particularly common on the 4G64 and 4G69 engines.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt, tensioner, idler pulleys, and water pump as a complete kit every 60,000 miles. Use only OEM or premium aftermarket timing components. Do not reuse the old hydraulic tensioner.
symptoms: Squealing or chirping from timing cover
Coolant leak from water pump weep hole
Engine misfiring or rough running

records.title: Automatic Transmission Failure (4-Speed)
records.description: The 4-speed automatic transmission in the 3rd generation Eclipse (particularly V6 GT models) is prone to premature failure. The transmission develops harsh shifting, slipping, and eventually fails completely, often due to overheating and worn clutch packs.
records.solution: Install an auxiliary transmission cooler to prevent overheating. Change the ATF every 30,000 miles. When the transmission fails, consider a quality remanufactured unit from a Mitsubishi specialist.

records.title: Valve Stem Seals Hardening - Oil Consumption and Blue Smoke at Idle
records.description: As the 4G63/4G63T ages, the valve stem seals harden and shrink, letting oil seep down the valve guides into the combustion chamber. The signature symptom is a puff of blue smoke on startup or on a quick rev after the engine has idled for a while, plus gradual oil consumption. Turbo cars can also show smoke that is confused with turbo seal failure, so proper diagnosis matters. This is a wear/age issue rather than a design defect and is very common on high-mileage 1G and 2G cars.
records.solution: Confirm the source (valve seals vs. turbo seals vs. worn rings) with a leak-down/compression test and by watching when the smoke appears. Replace the intake and exhaust valve stem seals; on the 4G63 this can be done with the head on the engine using a valve-spring compressor and compressed air to hold the valves, which greatly reduces labor. If oil control rings or guides are also worn, a head rebuild is required.
symptoms: Blue smoke on cold startup
Puff of smoke when revving after idling
Gradual oil consumption between changes
Oil fouling of spark plugs
Smoke on deceleration/overrun

records.title: AC Compressor Premature Failure
records.description: The Endeavor shares the same AC compressor platform as other Mitsubishi models of the era, and it is equally prone to premature failure. The compressor clutch and internal seals fail between 60,000 and 90,000 miles.
records.solution: Replace the compressor assembly with the receiver/drier and expansion valve. Flush AC lines and use the correct refrigerant charge. An OEM-quality aftermarket compressor provides good longevity at lower cost.

records.title: Automatic Transmission Harsh Shifting and Failure
records.description: The Endeavor 4-speed automatic transmission develops harsh shifting and premature wear, often failing between 100,000 and 130,000 miles. The transmission shares components with the Galant and Eclipse platforms, inheriting their reliability weaknesses.
records.solution: Perform ATF changes every 30,000 miles. Install an auxiliary cooler for vehicles used for towing. A quality remanufactured transmission with updated clutch packs is the best repair option.

Delayed reverse engagement
Overheating during towing

records.title: A/C Condenser Failure with Refrigerant Leak
records.description: 2004-2012 Galants suffer recurring A/C condenser failures — the OEM condenser had thin tube walls that develop pinhole leaks, especially in salt-belt climates where road salt accelerates corrosion. Mitsubishi released multiple part revisions through mid-2010 but failures continued. Symptoms: gradual loss of A/C cooling, oil residue around the condenser, low-side pressure too low on gauges. Replacement runs $400-$800 parts + 2-3 hours labor; aftermarket condensers (Denso, Spectra) work well.
records.solution: Replace the compressor, receiver/drier, and expansion valve. Flush the system thoroughly to remove any debris. Use the correct PAG oil specification for the replacement compressor.
symptoms: AC not cooling
Grinding noise from AC compressor
Intermittent AC operation
Low refrigerant warnings

records.title: Cracked plastic radiator end tank / overheating
records.description: Like many 1990s Mitsubishis, the Galant uses a radiator with plastic end tanks that grow brittle with age and heat-cycling. The top tank is a very common crack point, producing coolant loss, steam, and overheating. On the turbo 4G63 an overheating event is especially damaging because it can lead to head-gasket failure and warping. Enthusiast community guides call the cracked top tank a frequent, expected age-related failure and recommend switching to an all-metal radiator.
records.solution: Replace the radiator when the plastic tank cracks; an all-aluminum radiator is the recommended upgrade for durability. Address any coolant loss promptly and inspect hoses and the water pump (which is behind the timing cover) at the same time to avoid overheating damage.
symptoms: Coolant loss / puddles under the front
Steam or coolant smell
Temperature gauge climbing / overheating
Visible crack or seepage at the top radiator tank seam

records.title: Crankshaft position sensor failure causes stalling / no-start
records.description: The crankshaft position sensor on the 2.4L (4G64) Galant fails with age and heat, sometimes intermittently. Because the ECU uses this signal to fire spark and injection, a failing sensor typically produces a hard-start, an engine that cranks but will not start (often after the engine warms up), or sudden stalling while driving, frequently with the check-engine light on. The sensor is a three-pin Hall-effect unit mounted to the front of the engine reading a trigger plate.
records.solution: Test the sensor per the diagnostic procedure (resistance/signal check) and replace if out of spec. It is an inexpensive part with about an hour of labor. A no-start with codes P0335/P0340 should prompt inspection of both the crank and cam sensors and confirmation that the timing belt has not jumped a tooth.

records.title: Premature automatic transmission failure (slipping, harsh/failed shifts)
records.description: The 4-speed automatic in the 1990s Galant is prone to premature internal failure, especially when the fluid is never serviced and no auxiliary cooler is fitted. Documented failure modes include slipping (notably losing drive or slipping in reverse), harsh or delayed 2-3 shifts, flaring, and eventual loss of a gear as clutch packs and valve-body components wear and hydraulic pressure drops. RepairPal lists premature automatic failure as a recognized Galant complaint pattern.
records.solution: Preventively service the fluid and filter on a regular interval and add a transmission cooler for hot-climate or towing use. Once slipping/failure has set in, the accepted repair is a valve-body service or a full rebuild/replacement of the transmission. Some units also need an adaptive-shift reset after valve-body work.

records.title: Timing belt / balance shaft belt failure destroys interference engine
records.description: The 4G63 (2.0L) and 4G64 (2.4L) four-cylinders in the 1990s Galant are interference engines driven by a rubber timing belt on a strict 60,000-mile / 7-year replacement interval. On a neglected belt the valves collide with the pistons the instant the belt lets go, bending valves and often cracking piston crowns. A well-documented secondary failure mode is unique to this engine family: the smaller balance-shaft belt (which spins the counter-rotating balance shafts) shreds first, and the debris can be pulled into the main timing belt, snapping it and taking out the valvetrain. Because of this, the balance-shaft belt and its tensioner should always be replaced together with the main timing belt.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt, balance-shaft belt, water pump, tensioner, and idler pulleys as a complete kit every 60,000 miles or 7 years. Never reuse the old tensioners/pulleys. If the belt has already broken, expect a cylinder-head rebuild (bent valves, valve guides, possibly pistons) or a replacement long block.

Sudden loss of power while driving
Engine cranks but will not start after belt breaks

records.title: 4-Speed F4A4 / 5-Speed Sportronic Automatic Transmission Failure
records.description: 9th-gen Galant transmissions develop two distinct failure patterns: the 2.4L I4 cars use the F4A4 4-speed (torque converter clutch shudder, harsh shifts after ~100k miles) and the V6 Sport/Ralliart use the W5A51 5-speed Sportronic (3rd-gear clutch pack failure, solenoid issues). Both are repairable but expensive. Mitsubishi did not issue an extended warranty for either failure mode; the V6 5-speed failures are particularly costly due to less aftermarket support.

records.title: Valve cover gasket and valve stem seal oil leaks (burning-oil smell)
records.description: As the Galant's 4G63/4G64 engines age, the valve cover gasket hardens and leaks oil onto the exhaust manifold, producing a burning-oil smell after warmup and oil pooling in the spark plug wells (which can cause misfires). A related age issue is hardened valve stem seals, which let oil seep past the valves while the engine is off and produce a puff of blue/white smoke on startup. Both are common, low-severity wear items on these high-mileage engines.
records.solution: Replace the valve cover gasket (and spark plug tube seals) to stop the external leak; this is a low-cost job. For valve-stem-seal-related startup smoke, replace the stem seals - possible with the head on the block but labor-intensive because the valve springs must be compressed in place.

records.title: 4B11 Timing Chain Stretch

records.title: CVT Reliability and Longevity Concerns
records.description: The Jatco CVT in the Mirage exhibits premature wear and reduced longevity, with some units failing as early as 60,000 miles. The small displacement engine works hard to move the vehicle, putting additional stress on the CVT belt and pulleys.
records.solution: Change CVT fluid every 25,000-30,000 miles using Mitsubishi-specified fluid. Avoid full-throttle launches and sustained high-RPM driving. If the CVT begins slipping, replacement is more economical than rebuilding.

records.title: Automatic Transmission Torque-Converter Lockup Shudder and Slipping
records.description: The Aisin-based 4-speed automatic (V4AW2/V4AW3) behind the Montero V6 develops a torque-converter lockup (damper-clutch) shudder as it ages, felt as a vibration or 'buzz' typically in the 35-50 mph range at steady throttle that owners often mistake for an engine misfire. A Mitsubishi TSB attributes this to breakdown of the ATF causing damper-clutch shudder (documented for 1999-2003 Montero/Montero Sport; on RWD trucks it can also cause rear leaf-spring chatter). Neglected or overheated fluid, common on trucks that tow or wheel, also leads to worn clutch packs, slipping, delayed engagement, and harsh or missed shifts.
records.solution: Start with the fluid: use the correct ATF, correct level, and inspect condition; a fluid service (and a friction-modifier additive in mild cases) frequently reduces or eliminates lockup shudder. Verify the throttle position sensor and transmission temperature/pressure inputs. Add or service an auxiliary transmission cooler on trucks used for towing/off-road. Persistent slipping or clutch-pack wear requires a transmission rebuild and torque-converter replacement.

records.title: Crankshaft Position Sensor / Distributor Pickup Failure (Crank-No-Start and Stalling)
records.description: The 6G72's crank/cam timing signal on early 1990s trucks is generated inside the distributor, and later trucks use a discrete crankshaft position sensor at the front of the engine behind the crank pulley/timing covers. As these sensors and their pickups age they fail intermittently, producing a classic 'cranks but won't start' condition or sudden stalling while driving that often clears after the engine cools. Owners repeatedly report that aftermarket sensors do not resolve the problem and that only a genuine Mitsubishi (OEM) sensor restores reliable operation; the crank sprocket tone/reluctor ring can also strip or be damaged.
records.solution: Test the crank sensor/ignition pickup output per the factory procedure before replacing parts. Replace the failed crankshaft position sensor (or the distributor pickup on early trucks) with a genuine OEM Mitsubishi unit, as aftermarket units are widely reported to be unreliable here. Inspect the crank sprocket/tone ring for stripping or damage. Address related ignition coil/power transistor faults that can mimic the same stall.

records.title: Transfer Case Failure
records.description: The Montero Sport transfer case develops internal bearing and chain wear, leading to grinding noises, difficulty engaging 4WD, and eventual failure. The transfer case fluid breaks down faster than the service interval suggests, accelerating wear.
records.solution: Change the transfer case fluid every 30,000 miles instead of the factory-recommended interval. Replace the transfer case chain and bearings when noise is detected. A quality rebuilt transfer case is available for complete failures.

records.title: Super Select 4WD Vacuum Actuator / Free-Wheel Engagement Failure
records.description: The Montero's Super Select 4WD (second-generation, 1992+) engages the front axle through a vacuum-operated free-wheel actuator and electric solenoids rather than a mechanical linkage from the shifter. Over decades the dual-solenoid pack fails, the rubber hoses deteriorate, and the front differential actuator (a small shaft under a rubber boot on the passenger side of the front diff) can rust or seize, especially after long storage. The result is a truck that will not engage or disengage 4WD properly, gets stuck in 2WD or 4WD, grinds from the front axle, or flashes the 4WD indicator lights. This is a signature, well-documented failure mode discussed extensively in the overland/Expedition Portal community.
records.solution: Diagnose with a hand vacuum pump: apply vacuum to the free-wheel actuator, confirm it strokes fully into 4WD and holds vacuum. Replace failed 4WD select solenoid valves, cracked vacuum hoses, and a rusted vacuum reservoir; free or replace a seized front-axle actuator. Verify the front-axle detection switch and transfer-case position switches, and clean/reseal connectors. On later/OBD-II trucks, read the transfer-case control codes to isolate the failed component.
symptoms: 4WD will not engage or will not release
Front-wheel/4WD indicator lights flashing
Stuck in 2WD or stuck in 4WD
Grinding noise from the front axle on engagement
Difficulty shifting the transfer case between ranges

records.title: Timing Belt Failure on Interference Engine (6G72/6G74) Causes Bent Valves
records.description: Both the 3.0L 6G72 and the 3.5L 6G74 V6s used in the 1990s Montero are interference-design engines driven by a rubber timing belt. If the belt snaps, or if it is contaminated by oil leaking from the front cover/cam seals, the pistons strike the open valves and bend them. Note that while the generic 12-valve SOHC 3.0L in some Chrysler/Dodge applications is often called non-interference, the 6G72 as installed in the Mitsubishi Montero/Diamante is confirmed by engine references and owners to be an interference motor, and the 6G74 is interference as well. Many 90s Monteros are now well past any documented belt service, making this the single most consequential neglected item on the platform.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt on the factory interval (roughly every 60,000 miles / ~7 years), and replace the tensioner, idler, and water pump at the same time since they share the same access. Fix any front cover or cam/crank seal leaks that could oil-soak the belt. If a belt has already broken, install a new belt/tensioner set and perform a compression or borescope check for bent valves before returning the engine to service; bent valves require head removal and valve replacement.

Sudden loss of power while driving
Rattling or slapping noise from front timing cover before failure
Rough running or dead cylinders after a belt event
Low or zero compression on affected cylinders

records.title: Valve Stem Seal Wear and High Oil Consumption on High-Mileage V6s
records.description: As the 6G72 and 6G74 V6s age, the valve stem seals harden and crack and the piston rings/valve guides wear, allowing oil into the combustion chamber. This is one of the most widely reported 90s Montero engine complaints. Owners report consumption on the order of a quart every 1,000-1,500 miles with bluish smoke that is worst on cold startup (after the engine sits, oil seeps past the seals and burns off in a plume) and on deceleration. Note that the underlying cause is often worn valve guides, so seal replacement can be a band-aid; Mitsubishi's own spec treats ~1 quart/1,000 miles as within range for this engine family.
records.solution: Replace the valve stem seals (often done with the heads on using a spring compressor and air-hold tool, otherwise heads are removed) and inspect the valve guides, since worn guides are the frequent root cause. Confirm the source with a leak-down test to distinguish seals/guides (smoke mainly on startup/decel) from worn rings (smoke under load/all the time). Verify PCV system operation; if rings are the cause, plan for a more involved rebuild.
symptoms: Blue/gray smoke from exhaust on cold startup
Puff of smoke on deceleration or after idling
Elevated oil consumption (roughly a quart every 1,000-1,500 miles)

records.title: 12V Auxiliary Battery Parasitic Drain / Repeated Dead Battery
records.description: Fourth-generation Outlander and Outlander PHEV owners (2022+) report the 12V auxiliary battery repeatedly going flat, sometimes leaving the car dead in a day or two, even on nearly new vehicles and with the traction battery fully charged. Identified culprits on owner forums include the OEM infotainment/radio head unit failing to fully sleep, a driver's seat control module intermittently drawing current, a WiFi/telematics module, and a charging logic that tops up the 12V battery on a fixed daily timer rather than by voltage - so a low battery may never recover. Distinct from the high-voltage traction-battery issues.
records.solution: Diagnose parasitic draw with a multimeter (fuse-pull method) to isolate the offending circuit; check for infotainment/seat-module software updates at the dealer. Replace a degraded 12V battery (vented AGM type on PHEV) and verify DC-DC/alternator charging. Some owners fit a battery maintainer for vehicles parked for extended periods. Dealers have addressed specific VINs with module reprogramming.

records.title: AC Compressor Failure
records.description: The AC compressor in the Outlander is prone to premature failure, with the internal clutch bearing seizing or the compressor developing internal leaks. Failure typically occurs between 60,000 and 90,000 miles, leaving the vehicle without air conditioning.
records.solution: Replace the AC compressor, receiver/drier, and expansion valve as a complete system. Flush the AC lines to remove debris from the failed compressor. Use the correct PAG oil specification for the replacement unit.
symptoms: AC blowing warm air
Clicking or grinding from compressor
Intermittent cooling
Refrigerant leak detected

records.title: CVT Transmission Premature Failure
records.description: The Jatco CVT in the Outlander is prone to premature failure, particularly under heavy loads and in hot climates. The CVT belt and pulleys wear prematurely, leading to slipping, shuddering, and eventual complete transmission failure, often between 60,000 and 100,000 miles.
records.solution: Change CVT fluid every 30,000 miles using Mitsubishi DiaQueen CVTF-J4. Avoid aggressive driving and towing near maximum capacity. If the CVT fails, replacement with a remanufactured unit is more cost-effective than rebuild.
symptoms: Transmission shuddering during acceleration
Loss of power at highway speeds
Whining noise increasing with speed
CVT overheating warning

records.title: Engine Malfunction / 'Power Reduced' Warning from ECU Software (False P0401/P0404, TSB-22-13-001)
records.description: Early 2022 Outlanders with the 2.5L engine can illuminate the check-engine light and display an 'Engine malfunction / Power reduced — service now' message while idling or driving, often storing EGR-related codes (P0401/P0404) that do not reflect an actual hardware fault. Mitsubishi traced this to engine-ECU control software and issued TSB-22-13-001 to reflash the ECU with countermeasure software on vehicles built before December 16, 2021.
records.solution: Have the dealer reprogram the engine ECU per Mitsubishi TSB-22-13-001 (perform the reflash first, then re-diagnose only if codes persist). The update corrects the false low-EGR-flow detection so the warning and limp-mode no longer trigger spuriously.
symptoms: Check-engine light illuminates
'Engine malfunction power reduced service now' dashboard message
Reduced power / limp mode while idling or driving
EGR-flow trouble codes that return after clearing

records.title: Fuel Pump Failure Causing Engine Stall (Recall 22V027)
records.description: NHTSA recall 22V027 (Mitsubishi campaign SR-22-001) covers ~16,600 2022 Outlanders whose in-tank fuel pump has a commutator and internal wires that may be fused incorrectly during manufacturing, causing the pump to fail. A failing fuel pump can starve the engine and cause an unexpected stall while driving, raising crash risk. This is a manufacturing/supplier defect, separate from any CVT-related stall concern.
records.solution: Check the VIN against NHTSA recall 22V027 (Mitsubishi SR-22-001 fuel pump campaign) and have the dealer replace the defective fuel pump free of charge. Warning signs of an impending failure include hard starting, sputtering, or loss of power under acceleration.
symptoms: Engine stalls or shuts off while driving
Hard starting or extended cranking
Sputtering or hesitation under acceleration
Sudden loss of power

records.title: Hood Flutter and Bounce at Highway Speed (Latch/Weatherstrip Defect)
records.description: 4th-gen Outlander owners report the hood visibly flutters, shakes, and bounces at highway speed or in strong headwinds, feeling as though it could unlatch and fly open. The defect stems from the hood-latch/bumper-stop design and weatherstripping; Mitsubishi issued a TSB (latch/bumper-stop adjustment, weatherstrip and later reinforced-hood replacement) that owners report did not reliably resolve it, and a class-action lawsuit over the defect proceeded and reached a preliminary settlement.
records.solution: Have the dealer perform the Mitsubishi hood TSB (hood-latch and bumper-stop adjustment, weatherstrip replacement, and in later revisions a reinforced-hood replacement). If flutter persists, document it with NHTSA and check eligibility under the Outlander hood-defect class-action settlement, since the published fix was widely reported as incomplete.
symptoms: Hood shakes or flutters at 50+ mph
Hood bounces in strong headwinds or over bumps
Visible gap or movement at the leading edge of the hood
Sensation the hood could pop open while driving

records.title: Infotainment System Freezing and Connectivity Issues
records.description: The new-generation Outlander infotainment system experiences screen freezing, wireless Android Auto/CarPlay disconnections, and slow response to touch inputs. The system occasionally requires a vehicle restart to recover from a frozen state.
records.solution: Update to the latest firmware via USB or dealer. Perform a factory reset to clear corrupted data. Use wired connections for CarPlay/Android Auto if wireless connections are unreliable.
symptoms: Touchscreen freezing
Wireless phone projection disconnecting
Slow menu navigation
Backup camera delayed display

records.title: Phantom / False Automatic Emergency Braking (Forward Collision Mitigation)
records.description: Multiple NHTSA complaints describe the Outlander's Forward Collision Mitigation system warning and applying hard automatic braking with no obstacle present, including a 2022 SEL that decelerated from 70 mph and another that slowed itself without driver input. False triggers occur on highway curves and in rain or heavy dew that confuse the radar/camera sensors, creating rear-end collision risk.
records.solution: Update the ADAS/FCM software at the dealer and have the front radar and windshield-mounted camera inspected, cleaned, and recalibrated. Drivers can temporarily disable Forward Collision Mitigation where false activations are dangerous, but a software update/recalibration is the proper remedy.
symptoms: Automatic emergency braking with no vehicle ahead
Sudden hard braking on open highway or curves
False collision warnings in rain or heavy dew
System misreads vehicles in adjacent lanes as directly ahead

records.title: PHEV Battery Degradation and Charging Issues
records.description: The Outlander PHEV can experience accelerated battery capacity degradation and intermittent charging failures. The battery management system occasionally refuses to initiate charging or terminates sessions prematurely, particularly in extreme temperatures.
records.solution: Avoid frequent DC fast charging to preserve battery health. Keep the battery between 20-80% state of charge for daily use. Update the BMS software at the dealer. Have the 12V auxiliary battery tested, as a weak 12V battery can cause charging failures.
symptoms: Electric range decreasing over time
Charging session failing to start
Battery temperature warning
Reduced EV mode availability in cold weather

records.title: Rearview Backup Camera Image Blank or Frozen (Recalls 23V345 / 25V369)
records.description: A software error in the in-vehicle infotainment unit (A-IVI) can cause the rearview/backup camera image to freeze or fail to appear when reverse is selected, because external electrical noise or voltage fluctuation prevents the head unit from receiving the camera signal. This non-compliance with FMVSS 111 led to NHTSA recall 23V345 (2022-2023 Outlander + 2023 PHEV), later superseded and expanded by 25V369 (~200,000 units, 2022-2024 Outlander + 2023-2025 PHEV).
records.solution: Have the dealer reflash the A-IVI / rearview-camera software under recall 23V345 (Mitsubishi SR-23-001) or the superseding 25V369 (SR-25-001), free of charge. Confirm coverage by VIN, since the expansion added later build dates and PHEV models, and vehicles fixed under 23V345 must have the new remedy applied.
symptoms: Black screen when shifting into reverse
Backup camera image freezes on a previous frame
Rearview image fails to appear or flickers
Camera works intermittently

records.title: Seat Belt Automatic Locking Retractor Deactivates Early (Child-Seat Recall 21V596)
records.description: NHTSA recall 21V596 (Mitsubishi SR-21-007) covers ~3,735 2022 Outlanders in which the Automatic Locking Retractor in the right-front and both second-row seat belts can deactivate before the webbing is fully retracted, preventing a child restraint from being cinched tight. The cause is an out-of-spec bearing plate inside the retractor. The vehicles fail to meet FMVSS 208, increasing injury risk to a child in a crash.
records.solution: Verify the VIN against NHTSA recall 21V596 (Mitsubishi SR-21-007) and have the dealer inspect and, as needed, replace the right-front and both second-row seat belt assemblies free of charge.
symptoms: Child seat cannot be cinched tight with the seat belt
Seat belt does not stay locked when fully extended
Belt retracts/loosens after locking for a child restraint

records.title: Spontaneous Windshield and Door Glass Cracking (4th-Gen Thin Glass)
records.description: Fourth-generation Outlander (2022+, GN platform shared with Nissan Rogue) owners report windshields and side door glass cracking spontaneously or from minor road impacts, often within the first weeks of ownership. NHTSA complaints and CarComplaints entries describe cracks appearing with no visible rock strike, including glass cracking while the vehicle sits in a driveway, and multiple owners describe the OEM glass as thin/'cheap.' Because the windshield houses the forward camera for Forward Collision Mitigation and lane assist, replacement requires ADAS recalibration, driving cost well above a standard windshield.
records.solution: No recall or TSB addresses the glass quality; replacement is the only fix. Owners use insurance/comprehensive glass coverage. Aftermarket OEM-equivalent windshields plus mandatory ADAS camera recalibration; some owners report better durability with aftermarket laminated glass. Document repeat cracks for potential goodwill/lemon claims.
symptoms: Windshield crack appears with no known impact
Long cracks spreading from edge of glass
Front driver or passenger door glass cracking while driving
Crack appearing within first weeks of ownership
Stress cracks originating near the frit/edge band

records.title: AC Compressor Premature Failure
records.description: The AC compressor in the Outlander Sport frequently fails between 50,000 and 80,000 miles. The compressor clutch bearing seizes or the internal reed valves break, contaminating the AC system with metal debris.
records.solution: Replace the AC compressor, receiver/drier, and expansion valve. Flush the entire system to remove metal particles. Install an inline filter on the liquid line to protect the new compressor from residual debris.
symptoms: AC not cooling
Loud clicking from compressor
Intermittent AC function
Refrigerant leak

records.title: Accessory drive belt auto-tensioner flange cracks (belt detaches, engine stalls)
records.description: On 2011-2012 Outlander Sport vehicles with the 4B11/4B12 engine, the drive belt automatic tensioner flange can crack, allowing the accessory drive belt to detach. With the belt gone the battery stops charging and the engine can stall, losing power steering assist. The root cause was a lead-free bearing substituted into the tensioner during production.
records.solution: Free dealer replacement of the belt tensioner with an improved-shape part under recall 18V-069 / Mitsubishi SR-18-001 (a related earlier campaign, 14V-562 / SR-14-009, replaced the belt itself).
symptoms: squealing or chirping from the accessory belt
battery/charging warning light
loss of power steering assist
engine stall

records.title: Battery drain / dead battery and no-start
records.description: Owners of 2015-era Outlander Sport models report repeated dead batteries, including the vehicle failing to start after sitting for a weekend and batteries needing replacement multiple times within low mileage. A parasitic electrical drain (rather than a simply weak battery) is frequently the culprit, alongside the usual battery/alternator/starter failures.
records.solution: Test for a parasitic draw (disconnect the negative cable when parked; if it restarts after reconnecting, hunt the drain). Replace a weak battery or failing alternator/starter as confirmed. Some dead-battery cases on 2015 models may be addressed under warranty - ask the dealer.
symptoms: dead battery after sitting
repeated battery replacements
clicking or no crank when starting
intermittent electrical malfunctions

records.title: CVT Judder and Hesitation
records.description: The Outlander Sport CVT develops a judder during low-speed acceleration and deceleration. The transmission hesitates when pulling away from stops, and the simulated shift points feel rough and inconsistent.
records.solution: Replace the CVT fluid with Mitsubishi DiaQueen CVTF-J4 every 30,000 miles. A TCM reprogram may smooth out the shift calibration. Avoid towing with the CVT-equipped models.
symptoms: Judder during light acceleration
Hesitation from stop
Rough simulated shift points
CVT whining noise

records.title: CVT shudder, slipping, and premature failure
records.description: The Jatco-built CVT used across most Outlander Sport years is prone to shuddering, jerking, hesitation when shifting from park to drive/reverse, whining or whirring noise during acceleration, and slipping (engine revs without proportional acceleration). Degraded CVT fluid and belt/chain wear are the primary drivers, and neglected fluid accelerates failure. Powertrain is consistently the most-complained-about area in NHTSA data for this model.
records.solution: Replace CVT fluid on a shortened interval (roughly every 30,000-60,000 miles rather than 'lifetime'). Persistent shudder may require a valve body or full CVT replacement. Earlier model years had a separate recall (16V-563) for a CVT control module causing delayed gear engagement.
symptoms: shuddering or jerking during acceleration
hesitation shifting into drive or reverse
whining or whirring noise
RPM rises but car does not accelerate (slipping)

records.title: CVT software defect causes engine over-rev and stall at highway speed
records.description: On 2019-2022 Outlander Sport models with a CVT and a keyed (mechanical) ignition, a programming error in the CVT-ECU can misread a brief (0.1 second or longer) loss of the ignition power supply signal and command an erroneous gear ratio. At speeds above 62 mph this causes the engine to over-rev, which can drive a piston into an exhaust valve, permanently damaging the engine and causing it to stall while driving. Mitsubishi reported 31 engines needed replacement before the recall.
records.solution: Free dealer reflash of the CVT-ECU software under NHTSA recall 22V-563 / Mitsubishi SR-22-004. Owners should check their VIN at nhtsa.gov for an open recall; engines already damaged by the fault are repaired/replaced under the campaign.
symptoms: engine revs unexpectedly high above 62 mph
sudden engine stall while driving
loss of power at highway speed
check engine light

records.title: Front lower control arm / crossmember corrosion (Salt Belt states)
records.description: On 2013-2015 Outlander Sport vehicles sold or registered in Salt Belt states, the front crossmember can corrode from road-salt exposure to the point that a front lower control arm may detach, causing loss of vehicle control. The recall covers 23 states/DC where winter road salt is used.
records.solution: Free dealer inspection under Mitsubishi recall SR-21-001 (NHTSA campaign). Depending on corrosion level, a sealing/anti-corrosion agent is applied or the front crossmember is replaced at no cost. Owners can contact MMNA at 1-888-648-7820 or check VIN at nhtsa.gov.
symptoms: clunking or knocking from front suspension
visible rust on front crossmember
loose or wandering steering
control arm detachment

records.title: Rear parking brake caliper corrosion (parking brake binds/won't engage)
records.description: On 2013-2016 Outlander Sport models, water can penetrate the rear brake caliper lever boot and reach the parking brake operating shaft, corroding the caliper body and actuator shaft. If the shaft binds, the parking brake may fail to engage or disengage fully, allowing the vehicle to roll when parked on a slope.
records.solution: Free dealer inspection and repair under recall 18V-070 / Mitsubishi SR-18-002. Dealers replace the parking brake boot and lever or the caliper body as needed, plus the rear caliper piston assembly. A later related campaign (20V-741) also addressed this area.
symptoms: parking brake won't fully engage
parking brake stuck or won't release
vehicle rolls on an incline when parked
rear caliper drag or noise

records.title: Underbody and Subframe Rust/Corrosion
records.description: The Outlander Sport is susceptible to accelerated underbody rust and corrosion, particularly in salt-belt states. The rear subframe, fuel tank straps, and brake lines are the most affected areas, with rust perforation occurring in as little as 5-7 years.
records.solution: Apply rust-proofing undercoating annually in salt-belt areas. Inspect the rear subframe for structural integrity during routine maintenance. Replace corroded brake lines with stainless steel or coated replacements.
symptoms: Visible rust on underbody components
Brake line corrosion
Rear subframe structural weakness
Fuel tank strap deterioration

records.title: Windshield wiper motor/linkage water intrusion and corrosion
records.description: On 2011-2016 Outlander Sport models, water can leak into the area between the hood and windshield, damaging the wiper motor, and the wiper linkage ball joints can corrode. Either failure can render the windshield wipers inoperative, reducing visibility in rain or snow.
records.solution: Addressed under recalls 16V-792 (wiper motor water damage) and 18V-103 (wiper linkage corrosion); dealers inspect and replace affected components free of charge. Check VIN at nhtsa.gov for an open campaign.
symptoms: wipers stop working
wipers move slowly or intermittently
grinding noise from wiper mechanism
reduced visibility in rain

records.title: Front Suspension Clunking and Noise
records.description: The Outlander develops front suspension clunking and knocking noises over bumps and rough roads. Worn front stabilizer bar end links and strut mount bearings are the primary culprits, with noise appearing as early as 30,000 miles.
records.solution: Replace the front stabilizer bar end links and strut mounts. Inspect the lower control arm bushings while the suspension is apart. OEM replacement parts are recommended as some aftermarket components have fitment issues.
symptoms: Clunking over bumps
Knocking noise during turns
Rattling from front suspension
Noise worse on rough roads
